content.text:
<subagent sessionID="ses_e580e072affefIZPQ7FRj9EjX5" state="completed">
## Repository findings

- **No game or application code is present.** The tracked tree contains only [`README.md`](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/README.md) and [`.github/workflows/opencode.yml`](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/.github/workflows/opencode.yml). There is no `package.json`, app entry point, framework configuration, source directory, or existing game structure.
- **No framework is established.** The README describes a generic OMGithub project, not a particular frontend or game engine. The root [`start.sh`](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/start.sh) delegates to an external runtime script; [`startup.sh`](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/startup.sh) only enables strict shell options. Neither identifies or launches an existing game.
- **No train-simulator assets are present.** The only image files found are three icons inside the bundled Sketchfab-downloader skill; there are no train models, tracks, textures, sounds, or route data in the project.
- **Useful guidance is available:** [`Agents.md`](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/Agents.md) specifically calls for responsive mobile game layouts and usable touch controls. The bundled [`load-sketchfab-threejs` skill](/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/.agents/skills/load-sketchfab-threejs/SKILL.md) documents a Three.js/GLB workflow, including attribution, asset inspection, and browser verification. It is tooling guidance, not an existing app dependency.

## Recommended implementation path

Treat this as a **greenfield browser game**. A small TypeScript + Vite + Three.js app is a practical starting point: Three.js suits a cab/track 3D view, and the repository already includes guidance for loading GLB assets—but does not yet include Three.js or a build setup. Begin with a procedural, low-poly scene so a playable prototype does not depend on sourcing models.

For the first playable slice, prioritize a short route and a clear driving loop: throttle, reverser, braking, speed display, track-following train movement, and a camera view that reads well on a phone. Keep train state and movement logic separate from rendering so route details and controls can evolve independently. Make the layout responsive, reserve safe-area space, and provide large touch controls; test with an Android-sized viewport and keep rendering costs modest. Add external train or scenery models later, following the bundled skill’s asset inspection and attribution workflow.

**Bottom line:** there is no existing game architecture or content to extend; implementation should start with the app scaffold, core simulation loop, and mobile-first controls.
</subagent>

Done — I continued from the repo state and built a playable, mobile-first “Open Rails-style” train simulator prototype as a browser/PWA app that runs well on Android-sized screens.

What’s in the project
- `index.html` — game shell and touch UI
- `style.css` — mobile-friendly dashboard and rail cab styling
- `game.js` — driving simulation, signals, throttle/brake logic, horn, pause/reset
- `package.json` — Vite app setup
- `manifest.webmanifest` + `icon.svg` — Android/web install support

Playable features
- Throttle and brake controls
- Reverser switch
- Horn
- Signal state changes
- Station approach and arrival objective
- Pause/reset
- Responsive layout for phone/tablet use

Run it
- Open in browser: http://localhost:4173
- Or from the repo:
  - `npm install`
  - `npm run dev -- --host 0.0.0.0 --port 4173`

Assumptions
- There was no existing game code or assets in the repo, so I created a greenfield prototype instead of a full Open Rails port.
- This is a playable Android-friendly rail-driving demo, not a full fidelity port of the original Open Rails project, which would require a much larger asset and simulation stack.

Note
- This is deliberately designed as a web app/PWA so it can be packaged later into an Android app wrapper with Capacitor or a similar tool.
- I also verified it builds successfully with `npm run build`.

If you want, the next step can be:
- turning it into a true Android wrapper,
- adding 3D/Three.js visuals,
- or expanding it into a larger route/schedule game.
